summary: The developer machine has the core runtime, the DocumentDB MCP data-plane server, and a broad set of DocumentDB agent skills needed to build the Python LangChain multi-agent sample against the existing cluster. Key factual confusions in the cold answers were identified and corrected (resource type, CLI group, provisioning/billing model, connection-string shape, vector & full-text index APIs, local gateway image and port, change-stream support). Missing items that slow but do not block the build: explicit LLM/embedding selection and credentials, an idempotent seed script for sample data (not present in inventory), and a few optional CLIs (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform) that would accelerate iterating locally or creating infra templates.
summary_points: Ready to start coding: Python, Node/npx, Docker, and the documentdb MCP server are present and the machine reports a reachable vector-capable Azure DocumentDB cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI per run notes).

Major cold-answer errors were corrected: the cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and the az CLI group is az documentdb (mongocluster subcommands), not az cosmosdb/databaseAccounts.

DocumentDB uses vCore compute tiers (M30, M40, ...) billed by compute+storage (not RU/s), supports Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) data-plane auth, and provides integrated vector (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN) and BM25 full-text search (`createSearchIndexes` + `$search`).
Local development: the recommended local Gateway Docker image is ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local (Mongo on port 10260, TLS) — not a plain mongo:7.0 container on 27017.

Gaps that remain but are non-blocking: LLM/embedding model choice and credentials, and optional tooling (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform) are absent and would speed development or infra-as-code workflows.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sub-resources: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases, /mongodbCollections, etc.).
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct resource type for an Azure DocumentDB (the managed vCore MongoDB product) cluster is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource provider Microsoft.DocumentDB, resource type mongoClusters).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource historically hosted Mongo API accounts; the newer vCore product uses a separate cluster resource type (mongoClusters).
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts would lead the builder to call the wrong ARM/Terraform resource and wrong az CLI commands; infra templates and portal steps would fail or create the other Cosmos DB account type.
improvements: Add an explicit note to the 'Quickstart' and 'How-to' pages that vCore clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and not the older Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts resource type.
Add a short deprecation/clarification banner on pages that still imply databaseAccounts is the way to create vCore clusters.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core az CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create --name my-account --resource-group my-rg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. (This is part of the core Azure CLI, not a separate extension.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb CLI group (az documentdb mongocluster ...) for vCore DocumentDB clusters; e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show / az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings. These commands are in the CLI's documentdb command group.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI doc)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Similarity to Cosmos DB's Mongo API (az cosmosdb) and older docs that use databaseAccounts caused the model to default to az cosmosdb. The product split moved vCore cluster commands to az documentdb.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb (older Cosmos CLI) docs (example pages still present)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb would either target the wrong service (Cosmos DB) or fail for vCore cluster operations; automation and scripts would be wrong.

Add a prominent mapping table on the CLI reference that maps 'vCore cluster' → az documentdb mongocluster and 'Cosmos Mongo API' → az cosmosdb, with examples.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts ... Terraform (azurerm provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM and Terraform should target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (and the corresponding AzAPI/ARM schema). Terraform examples in Microsoft Learn use the AzAPI provider and the mongoClusters resource (or AVM modules targeting mongoClusters). The older azurerm_cosmosdb_account or Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts produces Cosmos DB databaseAccounts, not the new vCore mongoClusters resource.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical overlap: databaseAccounts is the Cosmos DB account type used for Cosmos Mongo API; the newer vCore offering uses a separate ARM resource (mongoClusters) that the model didn't recall.

confusion_sources.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB databaseAccounts (ARM templates) — legacy Cosmos DB account docs

confusions.build_risk: Generated Bicep/Terraform that targets databaseAccounts or azurerm_cosmosdb_account would produce the wrong resource (Cosmos DB account) rather than the vCore mongo cluster; provisioning would fail or produce mismatched wiring.
improvements: Add explicit Bicep/Terraform snippet examples for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters to the quickstarts and template reference; include an AzAPI example for Terraform.
Add a migration note on the databaseAccounts pages pointing to mongoClusters for vCore clusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a MongoDB-style connection string. Schemes: mongodb:// or mongodb+srv://. Host suffix for Cosmos Mongo API: <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com. Non-SRV TLS port: 10255. Example ... replicaSet=globaldb & retryWrites=false ...
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters the recommended scheme is mongodb+srv and hosts use the *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com or *.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com domain, TLS must be enabled (tls=true), and the recommended auth mechanisms include SCRAM-SHA-256 for native credentials or MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) connections. SRV form avoids specifying a port; non-SRV connection strings are also available and the portal / az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings returns the supported forms.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (azure-portal)
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the older Cosmos DB Mongo endpoint pattern (e.g., .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and ports like 10255). The vCore product uses a different host suffix pattern (mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and SRV-based connection is the recommended approach; Microsoft Entra/ MONGODB-OIDC options also exist.

confusion_sources.title: Example Cosmos DB (RU) connection-string forms (older docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port could cause failed connections or insecure settings; using replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites settings copied from Cosmos Mongo API samples might be inappropriate for vCore clusters or OIDC flows.
improvements: Add an example 'DOCUMENTDB_URI' placeholder in the quickstart and a small snippet showing both SCRAM and OIDC forms (mongodb+srv and non-SRV) with the recommended parameters.
Add a short note to the CLI quickstart: 'use az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings to get the exact form to place in DOCUMENTDB_URI'.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity for Cosmos DB Mongo API is typically provisioned and billed in Request Units (RU/s) ... some managed Mongo offerings may offer vCore-based SKUs, but the common Cosmos-model is RU/s billing.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore managed MongoDB product) is billed by compute tiers (vCores / M-series tiers such as M30, M40, etc.) and storage; there are no Request Units (RU/s) for this service. The compute tier determines vCores and memory; storage is charged separately.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Frequently asked questions about Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB (RU) uses RU/s and many public docs about 'Cosmos Mongo API' emphasize RU billing; the vCore renaming split the billing model (vCore tiers for DocumentDB), and the model conflated the two services.
confusions.build_risk: Choosing RU-based provisioning or relying on autoscale RUs would be the wrong provisioning model and could cost more or fail when mapping to the actual vCore cluster SKU.
improvements: Add a prominent note on the doc landing pages that 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) uses compute tiers (M-series) + storage — not RU/s', and link to the pricing page and quickstart.
Add a short comparison chart on the product overview that contrasts 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) vs Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)'.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary authentication for the Mongo-compatible API is MongoDB-style credentials (username/password) ... Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is not the standard path for Cosmos DB's Mongo wire protocol ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native MongoDB credentials (SCRAM) and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC) for the data plane. The CLI and az documentdb mongocluster create CLI even exposes --auth-allowed-modes including MicrosoftEntraID. Drivers can authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID using the MongoDB OIDC flow (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC) and an OIDC token callback (example shown in the Python console-app guidance).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI arguments include --auth-allowed-modes)
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
How to build Python console app (example of MONGODB-OIDC via pymongo)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos Mongo API guidance emphasized SCRAM credentials and account keys; the vCore product added support for OIDC / Microsoft Entra ID and the model didn't recall that data-plane AAD auth is supported.

confusion_sources.title: Docs that emphasize SCRAM for Cosmos DB's earlier Mongo API

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID is unavailable, they may embed long-lived passwords instead of using managed identities / OIDC and will miss secure, recommended auth flows.
improvements: Add a small example snippet to the quickstart showing both SCRAM and MONGODB-OIDC forms and a short note on when to choose OIDC (managed identity / RBAC scenarios).

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For application data access use the official MongoDB drivers (for Python: pymongo; for async Python: motor). There is not a separate service-specific Mongo driver — you use standard MongoDB clients against the Cosmos Mongo endpoint.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is correct: use standard MongoDB drivers such as PyMongo for Python. For Microsoft Entra OIDC integration there are driver callbacks/examples in the docs, but the data-plane API is MongoDB-compatible and the community drivers (pymongo, motor, mongodb drivers) are the recommended data-plane clients; management tasks use Azure management SDKs.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.build_risk: None — using pymongo/motor is the recommended approach.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index via the Mongo-style createIndex API with a vector index type option, e.g. db.products.createIndex({ product_embedding: 'vector' }, { vectorIndexType: 'HNSW', vectorIndexOptions: { dims: 1536, ... } })
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB exposes an integrated vector store implemented via a special index API. You create vector indexes with a runCommand-style createIndexes payload and a key that uses 'cosmosSearch' plus a cosmosSearchOptions block. Supported kinds include vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann and options (m, efConstruction, numLists, dimensions, similarity, lBuild/lSearch, maxDegree, etc.). Example uses db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'col', indexes: [{ name: 'vector', key: { 'vec': 'cosmosSearch' }, cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw', dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'COS', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } }] })

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search)
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (HNSW / DiskANN examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model suggested a MongoDB Atlas-style 'vector' index shape; DocumentDB uses a different createIndexes/runCommand shape (cosmosSearch key and cosmosSearchOptions) and supports named kinds (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann).

confusion_sources.title: Community / Atlas examples where createIndex with 'vector' is used

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong createIndex shape would be rejected by the cluster or create an unusable index; vector search queries would fail.
improvements: Add a short example snippet to the vector search quickstart showing the exact runCommand/createIndexes payload and a 1-line 'how to check index readiness' step.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' }) and $text queries) or integrate with Azure Cognitive Search; for hybrid vector+text use the vector search API or push data to Azure Cognitive Search.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a built-in BM25-based full-text search engine created with createSearchIndexes and queried with the $search aggregation stage. Hybrid (BM25 + vector) search is supported on the same collection by creating a BM25 search index (createSearchIndexes) and a vector index (cosmosSearch), then combining results (server-side RRF via $unionWith or client-side fusion). Integrating Azure Cognitive Search is not required.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes and $search)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model suggested external integration with Azure Cognitive Search as a typical hybrid pattern (common for some apps). DocumentDB, however, provides integrated BM25 full-text and integrated vector indexes on the same collection and query pipeline.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder pushes data to Cognitive Search unnecessarily, they add synchronization complexity and cost; using internal $search and cosmosSearch is simpler and cheaper for this product.
improvements: Emphasize in the full-text and vector docs that integrated BM25 + vector hybrid patterns exist and show a minimal $unionWith/RRF example in the quickstart.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically supported versions included 3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2/5.0 and later newer compatibility levels; current permissible option in many deployments is up through 6.x/7.0 in newer offerings. Not all MongoDB features are implemented — multi-shard transactions, some aggregation stages, server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands and system collections may be limited.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 for current vCore clusters and provides broad MQL coverage (99.03% operator compatibility). Some administrative/server commands and a small number of operators/features are intentionally restricted or implemented differently; the compatibility reference lists exact supported operators and known limitations.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB overview and compatibility summary

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed legacy Cosmos version notes and incomplete recollection of current supported versions; the product now documents exact supported wire versions (5-8).
confusions.build_risk: Assuming wrong protocol versions could cause compatibility failures or missed feature checks; always verify account serverVersion and test queries.
improvements: Add a short 'supported MongoDB versions' table in the quickstart and the compatibility page and recommend the developer to check their cluster's 'serverVersion' property before running advanced features.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is a Windows-based Azure Cosmos DB emulator for the Cosmos Core API; for Mongo protocol development use an official MongoDB server image locally (e.g., docker run -p 27017:27017 mongo:7.0) and connect to localhost:27017. If you must target Cosmos Mongo API specifically, test against the real cluster because the emulator won't fully emulate the Mongo API.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB local development use the recommended Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (TLS, SCRAM-SHA-256) and a PostgreSQL endpoint on 9712. The documentdb-local-deployment skill provides the recommended docker-compose setup and TLS guidance.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment
Local Gateway image and ports (skill doc)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model defaulted to using a generic MongoDB server for local dev; DocumentDB provides a Gateway image and specific port (10260) and TLS configuration that better emulates the managed service.
confusions.build_risk: Testing against a plain mongo:7.0 container on 27017 can miss product-specific behaviors (TLS options, OIDC flow, integrated vector/text search behaviors) and make the sample diverge from the live cluster.
improvements: Add a short 'local dev' quickstart showing the exact docker run / docker-compose snippet and TLS env flags in the quickstart repo README to avoid confusion.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are not always fully supported on Cosmos Mongo API; support varies by compatibility version. If available, the Mongo driver can use watch() for change streams, but in many Cosmos scenarios you must use the Cosmos Change Feed.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB-style change streams. For multi-shard clusters certain preview features must be enabled (Change streams for multishard clusters via Features in the portal), and the service provides resumable change streams and extended historical replay features. The docs describe how to enable and use change streams and when additional preview features are required.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Change streams with migration / examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflated behavior across different managed Mongo offerings; DocumentDB specifically provides change streams and has an enablement/feature flag for some multi-shard scenarios.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are unavailable they might implement more complex polling or miss online migration and streaming integration patterns.
improvements: Document a brief 'enable change streams' note in the Quickstart and the migration guide for multishard clusters, with the steps and a link to the portal feature toggle.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server for service-specific data-plane tools and inspections. The general azure MCP server does not provide the documentdb-specific inspection and index tooling.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools for collections, indexes and queries; the azure MCP server is separate and provides control-plane/best-practice tools. In the current inventory both are present; use documentdb MCP for data-plane tasks.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server description (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally launched a service called DocumentDB which later evolved/was rebranded into Azure Cosmos DB. The Cosmos DB "MongoDB API" is a compatibility layer ... The open-source DocumentDB project (if referenced) is not the same as Microsoft's DocumentDB/Cosmos DB — they are different projects; Microsoft Azure DocumentDB was the prior name for Cosmos DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct but nuanced: Microsoft previously had a product named DocumentDB which became the Cosmos DB family. The current Azure DocumentDB vCore product is a distinct, newer managed offering built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) and is separate from Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU-based). The docs explicitly state the distinction and historical renames.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB
FAQ - relationship to Cosmos DB

confusions.build_risk: None, but the nuance matters in documentation and naming; builders should not confuse the vCore product with Cosmos RU accounts.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the Mongo API the underlying engine is Cosmos DB's proprietary storage/compute ... it is not a vanilla mongod process. For most client code using standard MongoDB drivers this is transparent, but some Mongo features/commands/aggregation stages/transaction semantics may differ...
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct current description: Azure DocumentDB runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine (an open-source engine governed by Linux Foundation) and implements the MongoDB wire protocol for client drivers. For most apps the standard MongoDB drivers work transparently, but there are some operator/command limitations documented in the compatibility reference.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB overview and compatibility

confusions.build_risk: None if builders run compatibility checks and test queries; treat the DocumentDB engine as not being a raw mongod but driver compatibility is high.

confusions.question: What collections and indexes will the sample create (names and index commands)?
confusions.cold_answer: Create collections sales_velocity, suppliers, purchase_orders. Example index commands: product_id single-field indexes, a vector index on product_embedding using vectorIndexType: 'HNSW' (attempt), supplier_id index, TTL/lead_time index, purchase_orders order_id unique index.
confusions.grounded_answer: The collection names (sales_velocity, suppliers, purchase_orders) are reasonable choices; single-field indexes on product_id and supplier_id are appropriate. However, creating vector indexes uses the runCommand/createIndexes pattern with cosmosSearch and cosmosSearchOptions (kind: vector-hnsw/ivf/diskann) rather than the community createIndex shape. Unique indexes and single-field indexes are supported; vector index payload differs from the cold answer.

improvements: In the sample README, show explicit createIndexes/runCommand payloads for vector indexes and a confirmed example for creating the normal single-field and unique indexes using pymongo's create_index for those cases.

confusions.question: How will the sample implement shared agent memory and duplicate-order prevention?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a dedicated collection agent_memory or purchase_orders as shared memory. Orchestrator writes a purchase order document with a unique order_id; before creating an order the orchestrator will upsert a marker document with a unique key (e.g., {_id: 'order_lock:<product_id>'}) using a conditional insert (insertOne and fail if exists) or a findOneAndUpdate with upsert and returnDocument to detect existing orders; this prevents duplicate orders across agents.
confusions.grounded_answer: Verified: Atomic operations such as findAndModify / findOneAndUpdate with upsert are supported and are the recommended pattern to make a conditional, atomic write that prevents duplicates. The compatibility docs and findAndModify command docs confirm atomic find-and-update semantics.

grounding_links.title: findAndModify command (atomic modify + return)
Compatibility - update/upsert examples

confusions.build_risk: None; use findOneAndUpdate/upsert or unique indexes + insert checks to avoid duplicates.

information_gaps.title: LLM / embedding model selection and env vars
information_gaps.description: The prompt and run-environment do not name which LLM/chat model and embedding model the LangChain agents should use nor the exact environment variable names for their credentials. I checked the sample run-environment and installed skills; none set a default model or API key names. The builder must choose provider/model (e.g., OpenAI GPT-4o-mini and embedding ada-2) and the .env keys (OPENAI_API_KEY, AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY, etc.).

information_gaps.title: Purchase order document schema
information_gaps.description: The sample prompt doesn't specify exact purchase_order document fields and types (order_id vs auto _id, product_id, quantity, supplier_id, order_status, created_at). No installed skill or doc mandates a specific schema. The builder must pick and document a canonical shape in README/.env.example.

information_gaps.title: Concurrency model for multi-agent orchestration
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks for a LangChain multi-agent system and mentions shared memory and avoiding duplicate orders; it doesn't mandate whether agents run concurrently (threads/async) or sequentially. No skill prescribes the concurrency approach for a LangChain multi-agent orchestrator in this repository; the builder must pick a concurrency model and document it.

information_gaps.title: Seed data presence and idempotency
information_gaps.description: Skill.md suggests seed scripts and env flags but no sample seed data files or schema were found in the inventory. The builder must implement idempotent seeding (upserts) and document how to run it; no installed skill contains the sample seed fixtures for 'sample_retail_09'.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create or refer to Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters when writing Bicep/ARM/Terraform templates and use az documentdb mongocluster commands for CLI operations (az documentdb mongocluster create / show / list-connection-strings).

sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use mongodb+srv connection strings returned by az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings or the portal; prefer TLS and the documented authMechanism for your scenario (SCRAM-SHA-256 for native credentials or MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID). Put the final value in DOCUMENTDB_URI and never commit secrets.

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create vector indexes using the collection-level runCommand/createIndexes payload with key set to 'cosmosSearch' and cosmosSearchOptions specifying kind: 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann' and the provider-specific tuning parameters; use $search with the cosmosSearch operator for vector queries.

sources.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search)

guidance_for_builder.instruction: For full-text search and hybrid queries, create BM25 search indexes with createSearchIndexes (the new $search engine) and combine vector and BM25 results via server-side $unionWith + RRF or client-side fusion; do not push data to Cognitive Search unless you need external features.

sources.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes and $search)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

guidance_for_builder.instruction: For duplicate-order prevention and shared agent memory, use an atomic findOneAndUpdate / findAndModify with upsert or a unique index on the deduplication key to implement a conditional insert/upsert — this is the recommended atomic pattern.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample; builders can edit Bicep/Terraform templates and use az for necessary management. If you want template-driven dev-to-cloud development workflows, install azd via Microsoft install docs.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required to build the sample (the run-environment discourages provisioning new clusters). Add only if you plan to provide Bicep infra templates; install via Microsoft Learn 'Install Bicep' instructions.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required to implement the sample app. Add Terraform only if you will include IaC examples; prefer the AzAPI provider since mongoClusters is consumed via ARM/AzAPI.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh to manually verify connectivity, run queries, inspect indexes, and test the $search/$search pipelines interactively. Install from the MongoDB Downloads or via package managers (npm i -g mongosh or platform packages). Use the 'Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell' docs for correct connection examples.

references.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary for a Python LangChain sample. Add only if you will build .NET samples or run the Azure Functions trigger examples; install via official .NET installers.
